history.heading: An ancient land
paragraphs: The region of Palestine, between the Mediterranean and the Jordan River, has been inhabited since prehistoric times; Jericho is one of the oldest continuously inhabited cities in the world. Over the millennia it was home to Canaanites, Israelites, Philistines (from whom the name Palestine derives) and others, and was ruled by Egyptians, Assyrians, Babylonians, Persians, Greeks, Romans and Byzantines.

After the Arab conquest in the 7th century, the population became largely Arabic-speaking and Muslim, with Christian and Jewish communities. Jerusalem is holy to Islam, Christianity and Judaism. The region was part of the Ottoman Empire from 1517 to 1917.

history.heading: British Mandate and 1948
paragraphs: After the First World War, Britain governed Palestine under a League of Nations mandate. The Balfour Declaration of 1917 supported a Jewish national home, and Jewish immigration increased, leading to conflict with the Arab population, including the Arab revolt of 1936–39.

In 1947 the UN proposed dividing Palestine into Jewish and Arab states. In the 1948 war, following Israel's declaration of independence, about 700,000 Palestinians fled or were expelled from their homes, an event Palestinians call the Nakba. The West Bank came under Jordanian control and Gaza under Egyptian control.

history.heading: Occupation and the peace process
paragraphs: Israel occupied the West Bank, East Jerusalem and Gaza in 1967. The Palestine Liberation Organization (PLO), led by Yasser Arafat, became the main Palestinian representative. Two uprisings (intifadas) broke out, in 1987 and 2000. The 1993 Oslo Accords created the Palestinian Authority (PA) with limited self-rule, but a final peace agreement was never reached.

Hamas won elections in 2006 and took control of Gaza in 2007, splitting Palestinian governance. After Hamas led the 7 October 2023 attack on Israel, Israel's military campaign in Gaza killed tens of thousands of Palestinians, displaced most of Gaza's population and caused famine conditions and vast destruction. A ceasefire took effect in October 2025.

culture.heading: Identity and heritage
paragraphs: Palestinians are Arabic-speaking; most are Sunni Muslims, with a Christian minority. Millions of Palestinians live as refugees or in diaspora in Jordan, Lebanon, Syria and elsewhere. Bethlehem, birthplace of Jesus according to Christian tradition, and Hebron's old town are UNESCO World Heritage Sites.

Palestinian embroidery (tatreez) is recognised by UNESCO, and the dabke dance, olive trees and the keffiyeh are symbols of identity. Mahmoud Darwish is the national poet. Cuisine includes musakhan, maqluba and knafeh from Nablus.

politics.heading: The State of Palestine
paragraphs: The State of Palestine, declared in 1988, is recognised by about three-quarters of UN member states, with France, the United Kingdom, Canada, Australia and others recognising it in 2025. It is a UN non-member observer state. The Palestinian Authority, led by Mahmoud Abbas, administers parts of the West Bank, while Israel retains overall control, and Israeli settlements continue to expand.
No national elections have been held since 2006. The future governance of Gaza after the war and the two-state solution are at the centre of international diplomacy.

economy.heading: An economy under constraint
paragraphs: The Palestinian economy is heavily constrained by occupation, including restrictions on movement, trade and access to land and water. Agriculture (olives and fruit), small industry, services and work in Israel were key sources of income, along with foreign aid. Israel collects customs revenue on behalf of the PA, which it has at times withheld.
The war devastated Gaza's economy, and the West Bank economy has contracted sharply. The Israeli shekel is the main currency used.
